newsitem.title: UK: Spanish bonds set to outperform Italian BTP's.
newsitem.headline: Spanish bonds set to outperform Italian BTP's.

text.p: Spanish government bonds are set to outperform their Italian counterparts near term as improving fundamentals partially insulate them from EMU delay talk, analysts said on Thursday.
Fiscal austerity and better inflation data mean Bonos are a better bet than BTPs, which are groaning under the strain of political bickering and fears of a hitch to monetary union.
"When EMU delay risk increases, Italy suffers more than Spain," said Steven Major, head of bond research at Credit Lyonnais.
Mark Cliffe, chief international economist at HSBC Markets agreed Italy would likely bear the brunt of deconvergence trades on European Monetary Union (EMU) delay talk.

He said the 10-year BTP/Bund spread may bulge out to 250 basis points within the next few months, particularly if the Italian mini-budget continues to get bogged down by political squabbling. At 1340 GMT the spread was at 200 basis points.
Bonos will also be hit by talk of a postponement to EMU, but not as much.
"If Italy is trading 220 to 250 basis points over Bunds, the Spanish spread could go to 150-160 basis points," said Cliffe. By 1340 GMT the Bono/Bund spread was at 128 basis points.
BTP/Bund spreads billowed out by 12 basis points on Wednesday to 197 while Spanish bonds kept their cool and inched out only four basis points to 131.

Stephen Lewis, director of research at London Bond Broking, said since the crutch of EMU has effectively been taken away for the time being, peripheral countries were being judged on their fundamentals.
"And in that respect, Spain is doing much better than Italy," he said.

The Spanish inflation rate fell to 2.5 percent in February from 2.9 percent in January, but unemployment is still a hefty 14 percent. Spain's state deficit target for the year is 2.5 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), with three percent set for the full public sector.

"(Prime Minister) Jose Maria Aznar has succeeded in convincing investors that even if EMU were not on the horizon, he would still be a budget-cutter," said Lewis. "So there's more market confidence that Spain will stay on course and converge its economy with the rest of Europe."
Of the two peripheral European markets, analysts agreed they would plump for holding Spanish debt, but there was some disagreement about optimum duration.

"I would probably be relatively short as you'd have to be concerned about the long end suffering from Italian related problems," said Cliffe. But Lewis was more tempted by 10-year paper. "Even after the movements in recent days when Italy has lost more than Spain, I would prefer to be in the Spanish market," he said.
"I'd go for the 10-year area. Although we'll see some cuts in short term rates, there will be enough confidence long term to keep the long end stable," he said.
Credit Lyonnais' Major said there were still parts of the Italian curve -- at the short end -- which offered value.
"You're best out of the longer end of the curve in Italy," he said. "If you're going to be in, be in the shorter end, or position for curve steepening,"
But he added that if the possibility of Italy joining EMU within the next five years increased, investors should switch to the long end.
